### Behavior During Partition

**In Partition A** (AM-1 alone):
- AM-1 sees itself as position 0
- Waits 0 × timeout = 0 seconds
- Sends notifications (no dedup from AM-2/AM-3)

**In Partition B** (AM-2, AM-3):
- AM-2 is position 0, AM-3 is position 1
- AM-2 waits 0 seconds, sends notification
- AM-3 sees AM-2's notification log entry, deduplicates

**Result**: Duplicate notifications sent (one from Partition A, one from Partition B)

This is **intentional** - Alertmanager prefers duplicate notifications over missed alerts.
</source>

<source id="alertmanager/high_availability.md:1" doc="alertmanager/high_availability.md" title="High Availability" section="High Availability > Design Goals" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
## Design Goals

The Alertmanager HA implementation is designed around three core principles:

1. **Single pane view and management** - Silences and alerts can be viewed and managed from any cluster member, providing a unified operational experience
2. **Survive cluster split-brain with "fail open"** - During network partitions, Alertmanager prefers to send duplicate notifications rather than miss critical alerts
3. **At-least-once delivery** - The system guarantees that notifications are delivered at least once, in line with the fail-open philosophy

These goals prioritize operational reliability and alert delivery over strict exactly-once semantics.
</source>

```go
// Check notification log for recent sends

content.text:
This is actually **by design** and part of how Alertmanager prevents notification fatigue. Here's why you only see one notification instead of hundreds:

## How Alertmanager Groups Alerts

The **Alertmanager** handles alert routing, deduplication, and grouping automatically [D07:4]. It's configured to categorize similar alerts into a **single notification**:

> As a user, one only wants to get a single page while still being able to see exactly which service instances were affected. Thus one can configure Alertmanager to group alerts by their cluster and alertname so it sends a single compact notification [D07:5].

### During Large Outages

When many systems fail at once (hundreds or thousands of alerts), Alertmanager batches them intelligently:

- **Same alert type + cluster** = One notification [D07:7]
- **Example:** If dozens of instances of a service can't reach the database, they're grouped by `cluster=A` and `alertname=LatencyHigh` and sent as a single notification

### What You Control

You can customize grouping behavior via the routing tree configuration [D07:1]:

```yaml
# Group alerts by these labels
group_by: ['cluster', 'alertname']

# Or disable all grouping entirely
group_by: ['...']  # Passes through all alerts as-is
```

The system also has built-in deduplication logic that checks:
- Whether firing/resolved alerts changed
- Whether the repeat interval has elapsed
- Uses a replicated notification log across all nodes to avoid duplicate sends [D06:2]

**This isn't a limitation—it's an intentional feature** designed to help operations teams respond effectively during outages without being overwhelmed by hundreds of repetitive notifications.

Based on your company's alerting system documentation, here's why you receive only one notification instead of hundreds when many systems fail at once:

## Alertmanager Grouping

The key mechanism is **alert grouping**, specifically configured in your Alertmanager setup. The purpose of this design is stated clearly in the docs [D01:8]:

> "Grouping categorizes alerts of similar nature into a single notification. This is especially useful during larger outages when many systems fail at once and hundreds to thousands of alerts may be firing simultaneously."

### How It Works

When an outage occurs (like dozens or hundreds of service instances losing database connectivity), Prometheus would generate individual alerts for each affected instance. These alerts flow to Alertmanager, which then:

1. **Groups alerts** by cluster and alertname
2. **Consolidates them** into a single compact notification
3. **Shows details** about exactly which service instances were affected within that one message

For example, if network partition causes half of your service instances to lose database access, Alertmanager groups all those individual failures into one grouped alert rather than sending separate notifications for each instance.

### Benefits

This approach prevents:
- User inbox flooding
- Response paralysis from reading too many similar alerts
- Overwhelming notification delivery systems
- Wasted resources on redundant emails/slack/ PagerDuty notifications

While you get one consolidated notification, you can see all the specific affected instances listed within that single alert message, maintaining visibility without noise.

## Rate limits

Each key may make 60 requests per minute. Requests past the limit get HTTP 429 with error `REG-1009` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. Limits apply per key, not per agent, so two processes sharing one key share one limit.

Based on your company's alerting system documentation, here's why you receive only one notification instead of hundreds when many systems fail at once:

## Alertmanager Grouping

The key mechanism is **alert grouping**, specifically configured in your Alertmanager setup. The purpose of this design is stated clearly in the docs [D01:8]:

> "Grouping categorizes alerts of similar nature into a single notification. This is especially useful during larger outages when many systems fail at once and hundreds to thousands of alerts may be firing simultaneously."

### How It Works

When an outage occurs (like dozens or hundreds of service instances losing database connectivity), Prometheus would generate individual alerts for each affected instance. These alerts flow to Alertmanager, which then:

1. **Groups alerts** by cluster and alertname
2. **Consolidates them** into a single compact notification
3. **Shows details** about exactly which service instances were affected within that one message

For example, if network partition causes half of your service instances to lose database access, Alertmanager groups all those individual failures into one grouped alert rather than sending separate notifications for each instance.

### Benefits

This approach prevents:
- User inbox flooding
- Response paralysis from reading too many similar alerts
- Overwhelming notification delivery systems
- Wasted resources on redundant emails/slack/ PagerDuty notifications

While you get one consolidated notification, you can see all the specific affected instances listed within that single alert message, maintaining visibility without noise.

content.text:
This is because **Alertmanager uses grouping** to combine multiple alerts from similar systems into a single notification, which is especially important during large outages.

Here's how it works:

## Grouping Mechanism

According to the Alertmanager documentation, **grouping categorizes alerts of similar nature into a single notification**. This is especially useful during larger outages when many systems fail at once and hundreds to thousands of alerts may fire simultaneously [D07:2][A02:3].

For example, if dozens or hundreds of instances of a service are running in your cluster and a network partition occurs, where half of your service instances cannot reach the database, you'd get hundreds of individual Prometheus alerts. Alertmanager then consolidates these into fewer notifications based on common labels [A02:3].

## What Gets Grouped?

You can configure Alertmanager to group alerts by specific labels such as:
- **Cluster label**: Alerts grouped by which cluster the affected services are in
- **Alert name**: Alerts with the same metric/alert type (e.g., all "DatabaseConnectionError" alerts)

Multiple alerts coming in for `cluster=A` and `alertname=LatencyHigh` would be batched into a single group [C05:17].

## Why One Notification?

As a user, the goal is to get **one page** showing all affected systems while still being able to see exactly which service instances were affected [A02:3]. This prevents notification overload during major incidents and helps teams focus on investigating the root cause rather than processing hundreds of duplicate-looking alerts.

If you need more control over grouping behavior, you can adjust the routing configuration using the `<route>` section with custom `group_by` settings [C05:17].

This is because **Alertmanager uses grouping** to combine multiple alerts from similar systems into a single notification, which is especially important during large outages.

Here's how it works:

## Grouping Mechanism

According to the Alertmanager documentation, **grouping categorizes alerts of similar nature into a single notification**. This is especially useful during larger outages when many systems fail at once and hundreds to thousands of alerts may fire simultaneously [D07:2][A02:3].

For example, if dozens or hundreds of instances of a service are running in your cluster and a network partition occurs, where half of your service instances cannot reach the database, you'd get hundreds of individual Prometheus alerts. Alertmanager then consolidates these into fewer notifications based on common labels [A02:3].

## What Gets Grouped?

You can configure Alertmanager to group alerts by specific labels such as:
- **Cluster label**: Alerts grouped by which cluster the affected services are in
- **Alert name**: Alerts with the same metric/alert type (e.g., all "DatabaseConnectionError" alerts)

Multiple alerts coming in for `cluster=A` and `alertname=LatencyHigh` would be batched into a single group [C05:17].

## Why One Notification?

As a user, the goal is to get **one page** showing all affected systems while still being able to see exactly which service instances were affected [A02:3]. This prevents notification overload during major incidents and helps teams focus on investigating the root cause rather than processing hundreds of duplicate-looking alerts.

If you need more control over grouping behavior, you can adjust the routing configuration using the `<route>` section with custom `group_by` settings [C05:17].

No, it's generally **not OK** for two services to share one registry key.

According to the official documentation:

**Each key has a fixed rate limit that applies to all processes using it:**

- From the Registry API reference on rate limits [D01:8]: *"Each key may make 60 requests per minute. Limits apply per key, not per agent, so two processes sharing one key share one limit."*

- From the Agent owners' FAQ [D14:3]: *"Each key gets a fixed number of registry calls per minute. If two things share a key, say the agent and a dashboard, they share that allowance. Give the dashboard its own read-only key."*

**Why you shouldn't share keys:**
If multiple services share a single registry key, they compete for the same allocated request allowance. One service could exhaust the limit before another can make its requests, resulting in `HTTP 429` errors with error code `REG-1009`.

**Best practice:**
Give each service (especially independent tools like dashboards) its own dedicated registry key. Monitoring and dashboard tools should use read-only keys.

<source id="D14:3" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > Why does my agent get told to slow down?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">
## Why does my agent get told to slow down?

Each key gets a fixed number of registry calls per minute. If two things share a key, say the agent and a dashboard, they share that allowance. Give the dashboard its own read-only key.
</source>

<source id="D01:8" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Rate limits" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Rate limits

Each key may make 60 requests per minute. Requests past the limit get HTTP 429 with error `REG-1009` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. Limits apply per key, not per agent, so two processes sharing one key share one limit.
</source>

<source id="D08:4" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > Polling the registry from your own dashboards" date="2026-03-02" type="official">
## Polling the registry from your own dashboards

If you build your own dashboard on top of the registry, poll no more than once every few seconds. The registry allows 100 requests per minute per key, and a dashboard that uses most of that leaves nothing for the agent sharing its key.
</source>

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

<source id="D04:0" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > What the platform is" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## What the platform is

The agent platform is the set of services our agents run on. Agents are configured in the registry, look things up through shared services, and are watched by monitoring. This page describes the core services and how they connect. It doesn't cover every service an individual agent uses; each agent's owner documents those.
</source>

<source id="D04:0" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > What the platform is" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## What the platform is

The agent platform is the set of services our agents run on. Agents are configured in the registry, look things up through shared services, and are watched by monitoring. This page describes the core services and how they connect. It doesn't cover every service an individual agent uses; each agent's owner documents those.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/guides/dockerswarm.md:1" doc="prometheus-docs/guides/dockerswarm.md" title="Docker Swarm" section="Docker Swarm > Docker Swarm service discovery architecture" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
## Docker Swarm service discovery architecture

The [Docker Swarm service discovery][swarmsd] contains 3 different roles: nodes, services,
and tasks.

The first role, **nodes**, represents the hosts that are part of the Swarm. It
can be used to automatically monitor the Docker daemons or the Node Exporters
who run on the Swarm hosts.

The second role, **tasks**, represents any individual container deployed in the
swarm. Each task gets its associated service labels. One service can be backed by
one or multiple tasks.

The third one, **services**, will discover the services deployed in the
swarm. It will discover the ports exposed by the services. Usually you will want
to use the tasks role instead of this one.

Prometheus will only discover tasks and service that expose ports.
</source>

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

<source id="D14:3" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > Why does my agent get told to slow down?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">
## Why does my agent get told to slow down?

Each key gets a fixed number of registry calls per minute. If two things share a key, say the agent and a dashboard, they share that allowance. Give the dashboard its own read-only key.
</source>

<source id="D01:8" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Rate limits" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Rate limits

Each key may make 60 requests per minute. Requests past the limit get HTTP 429 with error `REG-1009` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. Limits apply per key, not per agent, so two processes sharing one key share one limit.
</source>

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

<source id="D14:3" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > Why does my agent get told to slow down?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">
## Why does my agent get told to slow down?

Each key gets a fixed number of registry calls per minute. If two things share a key, say the agent and a dashboard, they share that allowance. Give the dashboard its own read-only key.
</source>

<source id="D01:8" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Rate limits" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Rate limits

Each key may make 60 requests per minute. Requests past the limit get HTTP 429 with error `REG-1009` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. Limits apply per key, not per agent, so two processes sharing one key share one limit.
</source>

<source id="D12:0" doc="D12" title="Security postmortem SEC-014: registry key written to logs" section="Security postmortem SEC-014: registry key written to logs > Summary" date="2026-07-14" type="official">
## Summary

On 2026-07-11, a routine log review found `support_agent`'s write-scoped registry key in plain text in its debug logs. The logs are readable by about 60 engineers. The key was rotated within 3 hours of discovery. The registry's change history shows no use of the key from anywhere other than `support_agent` itself.
</source>

<source id="D06:0" doc="D06" title="Runbook: rotating a registry key" section="Runbook: rotating a registry key > When to rotate" date="2026-07-20" type="official">
## When to rotate

Rotate an agent's registry key every 90 days, and immediately if the key may have been exposed: written to a log, pasted in a chat, or committed to a repository. An exposed key is rotated first and investigated second.
</source>

answers:
To issue a registry key using regctl, use this command:

```bash
regctl keys issue --agent <agent_id> --scope <scope>
```

For example, based on our internal runbook [D06:1]:

```bash
regctl keys issue --agent support_agent --scope write
```

**Important notes:**
- `regctl` prints the new key once immediately after issuing it - you must store it in your secrets manager right away, as it cannot be shown again.
- Keys have a scope: `read` for GET endpoints only, or `write` for create/update/delete operations. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or person.
- The old key continues to work while the new one is issued, so agents won't be interrupted during rotation.

<source id="D06:1" doc="D06" title="Runbook: rotating a registry key" section="Runbook: rotating a registry key > Step 1: Issue the new key" date="2026-07-20" type="official">
## Step 1: Issue the new key

Issue a key with the same scope as the old one. The old key keeps working, so the agent isn't interrupted.

```bash
regctl keys issue --agent support_agent --scope write
```

`regctl` prints the new key once. Store it in the secrets manager straight away; it can't be shown again.
</source>

<source id="D06:4" doc="D06" title="Runbook: rotating a registry key" section="Runbook: rotating a registry key > Step 4: Revoke the old one" date="2026-07-20" type="official">
## Step 4: Revoke the old one

Revoke it within 24 hours of issuing the new one. Leaving both valid for longer doubles the number of keys that can leak. For an exposed key, don't wait: revoke as soon as Step 3 passes.

```bash
regctl keys revoke --key-id <old key id>
```

After revocation, anything still using the old key gets `REG-1003`. That's the signal that something was missed in Step 2.
</source>

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

<source id="D02:0" doc="D02" title="Error code reference" section="Error code reference > Authentication errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication errors

| Code | Name | HTTP | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `REG-1001` | `MISSING_KEY` | 401 | The request had no `X-Registry-Key` header. |
| `REG-1002` | `INVALID_KEY` | 401 | The key isn't one the registry issued. Check for a truncated or mistyped key. |
| `REG-1003` | `KEY_REVOKED` | 401 | The key was valid but has been revoked. Issue a new key; a revoked key can't be restored. |
| `REG-1004` | `FORBIDDEN_FIELD` | 403 | The key's scope doesn't allow this change. Writes need a `write` key. |
</source>

<source id="D06:1" doc="D06" title="Runbook: rotating a registry key" section="Runbook: rotating a registry key > Step 1: Issue the new key" date="2026-07-20" type="official">
## Step 1: Issue the new key

Issue a key with the same scope as the old one. The old key keeps working, so the agent isn't interrupted.

```bash
regctl keys issue --agent support_agent --scope write
```

`regctl` prints the new key once. Store it in the secrets manager straight away; it can't be shown again.
</source>

<source id="D06:4" doc="D06" title="Runbook: rotating a registry key" section="Runbook: rotating a registry key > Step 4: Revoke the old one" date="2026-07-20" type="official">
## Step 4: Revoke the old one

Revoke it within 24 hours of issuing the new one. Leaving both valid for longer doubles the number of keys that can leak. For an exposed key, don't wait: revoke as soon as Step 3 passes.

```bash
regctl keys revoke --key-id <old key id>
```

After revocation, anything still using the old key gets `REG-1003`. That's the signal that something was missed in Step 2.
</source>

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

<source id="D06:1" doc="D06" title="Runbook: rotating a registry key" section="Runbook: rotating a registry key > Step 1: Issue the new key" date="2026-07-20" type="official">
## Step 1: Issue the new key

Issue a key with the same scope as the old one. The old key keeps working, so the agent isn't interrupted.

```bash
regctl keys issue --agent support_agent --scope write
```

`regctl` prints the new key once. Store it in the secrets manager straight away; it can't be shown again.
</source>

<source id="D06:4" doc="D06" title="Runbook: rotating a registry key" section="Runbook: rotating a registry key > Step 4: Revoke the old one" date="2026-07-20" type="official">
## Step 4: Revoke the old one

Revoke it within 24 hours of issuing the new one. Leaving both valid for longer doubles the number of keys that can leak. For an exposed key, don't wait: revoke as soon as Step 3 passes.

```bash
regctl keys revoke --key-id <old key id>
```

After revocation, anything still using the old key gets `REG-1003`. That's the signal that something was missed in Step 2.
</source>

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

<source id="D02:0" doc="D02" title="Error code reference" section="Error code reference > Authentication errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication errors

| Code | Name | HTTP | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `REG-1001` | `MISSING_KEY` | 401 | The request had no `X-Registry-Key` header. |
| `REG-1002` | `INVALID_KEY` | 401 | The key isn't one the registry issued. Check for a truncated or mistyped key. |
| `REG-1003` | `KEY_REVOKED` | 401 | The key was valid but has been revoked. Issue a new key; a revoked key can't be restored. |
| `REG-1004` | `FORBIDDEN_FIELD` | 403 | The key's scope doesn't allow this change. Writes need a `write` key. |
</source>

Based on the company's runbooks and incident analysis, here's where slowdowns in agents typically come from:

## Primary Sources of Agent Latency

### 1. **Slow Tool Calls (Most Common)**
According to the agent latency spike runbook, **"most spikes come from one tool that got slow, not from the model"** [D05:2]. When investigating a latency issue:
- Open slow sessions and examine time spent in each tool call
- Tools are the usual culprit, not the AI model itself
- Common examples include external API calls (payments, auth-service), database queries, and search operations

### 2. **Cache Issues**
When using search tools:
- A cache hit rate below 40% indicates the cache was flushed or restarted
- Performance temporarily degrades while the cache refills (usually within 10 minutes)
- Persistent low hit rates after 10+ minutes suggest a misconfiguration [D05:3]

### 3. **Database Performance Problems**
For PostgreSQL-based systems, common culprits include:
- **WAL flush delays**: Checkpoint stalls when pages must be forced to disk instead of staying in OS page cache
- **Synchronous connection overhead**: Can cut performance by more than half over slow networks
- **Query complexity**: Expensive expressions aggregating over many time series

### 4. **External Service Failures**
As seen in incident INC-2041, external dependencies can cause cascading delays:
- Certificate expiry in upstream services causing timeouts
- Retry storms when agents treat intermittent failures as transient
- Timeouts masquerading as slow responses rather than errors [D09:2]

## Investigation Priority
The standard procedure recommends checking tool call breakdowns first, since the model is rarely the actual bottleneck during latency spikes. External service outages and cache misses are the other two most frequent causes.

## WAL Configuration

There are two commonly used internal WAL functions: `XLogInsertRecord` and `XLogFlush`. `XLogInsertRecord` is used to place a new record into the WAL buffers in shared memory. If there is no space for the new record, `XLogInsertRecord` will have to write (move to kernel cache) a few filled WAL buffers. This is undesirable because `XLogInsertRecord` is used on every database low level modification (for example, row insertion) at a time when an exclusive lock is held on affected data pages, so the operation needs to be as fast as possible. What is worse, writing WAL buffers might also force the creation of a new WAL segment, which takes even more time. Normally, WAL buffers should be written and flushed by an `XLogFlush` request, which is made, for the most part, at t

<source id="postgresql/wal.md:52" doc="postgresql/wal.md" title="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log" section="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log > WAL Configuration" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## WAL Configuration

On Linux and POSIX platforms section guc-checkpoint-flush-after allows you to force OS pages written by the checkpoint to be flushed to disk after a configurable number of bytes. Otherwise, these pages may be kept in the OS's page cache, inducing a stall when `fsync` is issued at the end of a checkpoint. This setting will often help to reduce transaction latency, but it also can have an adverse effect on performance; particularly for workloads that are bigger than section guc-shared-buffers, but smaller than the OS's page cache.

<source id="postgresql/wal.md:36" doc="postgresql/wal.md" title="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log" section="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log > Asynchronous Commit" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## Asynchronous Commit

The risk that is taken by using asynchronous commit is of data loss, not data corruption. If the database should crash, it will recover by replaying WAL up to the last record that was flushed. The database will therefore be restored to a self-consistent state, but any transactions that were not yet flushed to disk will not be reflected in that state. The net effect is therefore loss of the last few transactions. Because the transactions are replayed in commit order, no inconsistency can be introduced — for example, if transaction B made changes relying on the effects of a previous transaction A, it is not possible for A's effects to be lost while B's effects are preserved.
</source>

## Log-Shipping Standby Servers

The primary and standby server work together to provide this capability, though the servers are only loosely coupled. The primary server operates in continuous archiving mode, while each standby server operates in continuous recovery mode, reading the WAL files from the primary. No changes to the database tables are required to enable this capability, so it offers low administration overhead compared to some other replication solutions. This configuration also has relatively low performance impact on the primary server.
</source>

Metrics should only be pulled from the application when Prometheus
scrapes them, exporters should not perform scrapes based on their own

Pushgateway
instead.

a minute, it is acceptable to cache it. This should be noted in the

exporter can be expected to exceed this, you should explicitly call this
out in your user documentation.

## WAL Configuration

There are two commonly used internal WAL functions: `XLogInsertRecord` and `XLogFlush`. `XLogInsertRecord` is used to place a new record into the WAL buffers in shared memory. This is undesirable because `XLogInsertRecord` is used on every database low level modification (for example, row insertion) at a time when an exclusive lock is held on affected data pages, so the operation needs to be as fast as possible. What is worse, writing WAL buffers might also force the creation of a new WAL segment, which takes even more time. <source id="postgresql/wal.md:52" doc="postgresql/wal.md" title="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log" section="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log > WAL Configuration" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## WAL Configuration

On Linux and POSIX platforms section guc-checkpoint-flush-after allows you to force OS pages written by the checkpoint to be flushed to disk after a configurable number of bytes. Otherwise, these pages may be kept in the OS's page cache, inducing a stall when `fsync` is issued at the end of a checkpoint. This setting will often help to reduce transaction latency, but it also can have an adverse effect on performance; particularly for workloads that are bigger than section guc-shared-buffers, but smaller than the OS's page cache.

<source id="postgresql/wal.md:36" doc="postgresql/wal.md" title="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log" section="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log > Asynchronous Commit" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## Asynchronous Commit

The risk that is taken by using asynchronous commit is of data loss, not data corruption. If the database should crash, it will recover by replaying WAL up to the last record that was flushed. The database will therefore be restored to a self-consistent state, but any transactions that were not yet flushed to disk will not be reflected in that state. The net effect is therefore loss of the last few transactions. Because the transactions are replayed in commit order, no inconsistency can be introduced — for example, if transaction B made changes relying on the effects of a previous transaction A, it is not possible for A's effects to be lost while B's effects are preserved.
</source>

The primary and standby server work together to provide this capability, though the servers are only loosely coupled. The primary server operates in continuous archiving mode, while each standby server operates in continuous recovery mode, reading the WAL files from the primary. No changes to the database tables are required to enable this capability, so it offers low administration overhead compared to some other replication solutions. Based on the company's runbooks and incident analysis, here's where slowdowns in agents typically come from:

## Primary Sources of Agent Latency

### 1. **Slow Tool Calls (Most Common)**
According to the agent latency spike runbook, **"most spikes come from one tool that got slow, not from the model"** [D05:2]. When investigating a latency issue:
- Open slow sessions and examine time spent in each tool call
- Tools are the usual culprit, not the AI model itself
- Common examples include external API calls (payments, auth-service), database queries, and search operations

### 2. **Cache Issues**
When using search tools:
- A cache hit rate below 40% indicates the cache was flushed or restarted
- Performance temporarily degrades while the cache refills (usually within 10 minutes)
- Persistent low hit rates after 10+ minutes suggest a misconfiguration [D05:3]

### 3. **Database Performance Problems**
For PostgreSQL-based systems, common culprits include:
- **WAL flush delays**: Checkpoint stalls when pages must be forced to disk instead of staying in OS page cache
- **Synchronous connection overhead**: Can cut performance by more than half over slow networks
- **Query complexity**: Expensive expressions aggregating over many time series

### 4. **External Service Failures**
As seen in incident INC-2041, external dependencies can cause cascading delays:
- Certificate expiry in upstream services causing timeouts
- Retry storms when agents treat intermittent failures as transient
- Timeouts masquerading as slow responses rather than errors [D09:2]

## Investigation Priority
The standard procedure recommends checking tool call breakdowns first, since the model is rarely the actual bottleneck during latency spikes. External service outages and cache misses are the other two most frequent causes.

Based on the company's documentation, here are the typical sources of slowdown in agent latency investigations:

## Primary Sources of Latency

### 1. **External Service Dependencies** 
This is cited as the most common root cause. As noted in the monitoring practices: *"if you have a big tree of services in an online-serving system, latency in some lower service is a typical problem"* [D08:3]. Agents often call multiple external services (like payments gateways, auth services, databases), and latency usually comes from one of these downstream services timing out or being slow.

### 2. **Rate Limiting (REG-1009)**
Agents frequently encounter rate limits when calling external APIs:
- HTTP 429 responses with error `REG-1009` 
- Agents wait for the `Retry-After` header before retrying
- This waiting time accumulates across multiple API calls, making it look like high latency [D05:4]
- Rate limits apply per key, not per agent—so two processes sharing one key share the same limit [D01:8]

### 3. **Transient Errors Triggered Retries**
When external services timeout or fail:
- Agents treat timeouts as transient and retry until their step limit runs out
- Example from INC-2041: `"payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. billing_agent treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one"` [D09:2]

### 4. **Certificate/Infra Issues**
Infrastructure problems like expired intermediate certificates can cause authentication failures that result in upstream timeouts rather than clean errors [D09:2].

## Investigation Approach
According to the Runbook: agent latency spike, start by checking if the issue is real on the dashboard (p95 > 8 seconds for 10 minutes), then check the agent logs for REG-1009 rate limit responses, trace down to the external services involved, and escalate to the owning team once identified [D05:0][D05:1][D05:4][D05:5].

## Most Common Cause: External Tools
**Most latency spikes come from tools**, not the model itself. The runbook specifically states: *"Most spikes come from one tool that got slow, not from the model"* [D05:2]. When investigating, you should:

2. Analyze time spent in each tool call and model call
3. Identify which specific tool caused the spike

- **External Dependencies**: Third-party services or APIs being called by the agent

## What's NOT Usually the Problem:
The model typically isn't the source of latency spikes - it's the surrounding infrastructure and external calls that get stuck or slow down.

Based on the runbook and investigation procedures, here's where slowdowns usually come from in agent latency investigations:

**Most latency spikes come from tools**, not the model itself. The runbook specifically states: *"Most spikes come from one tool that got slow, not from the model"* [D05:2]. When investigating, you should:

- **Rate Limiting**: Agents receiving `REG-1009` responses will wait for `Retry-After` headers on every call, appearing as latency. Check if another process is sharing the agent's API key [D05:4].

- **Database/Infrastructure Issues**: Service-dependent issues like Postgres or other backend services

- **External Dependencies**: Third-party services or APIs being called by the agent

## What's NOT Usually the Problem:
The model typically isn't the source of latency spikes - it's the surrounding infrastructure and external calls that get stuck or slow down.

The investigation procedure is structured to help you identify these root causes systematically, starting with confirming the issue, then finding the slow step (tool vs model), checking for rate limiting, and escalating appropriately [D05:0-D05:5].

answers:
Based on the company's runbooks and incident reports, here are the most common sources of slowdown during agent latency investigations:

## Primary Causes of Latency

**1. Rate Limiting** [D05:4]
- Agents being rate-limited wait for `Retry-After` headers on every call, which appears as latency in metrics
- This often occurs when another process is sharing the agent's API key

**2. Timeouts Being Treated as Transient Issues** [D09:2]
- A frequent pattern: an external service times out (e.g., payments-gateway checking certificates with auth-service)
- The agent treats timeouts as temporary failures and keeps retrying until it hits its step limit
- Example from INC-2041: An expired intermediate certificate caused payment gateway timeouts, which billing_agent retried continuously

**3. Network Partitions**
- Can occur between services that need to communicate (e.g., alertmanager instances splitting during network partition)
- When services cannot reach databases or each other, requests fail or get stuck waiting

**4. Loop Bugs Without Step Limits** [D13:2]
- Historical example: a loop bug made billing_agent retry failed invoices indefinitely without a cap, exhausting $2,900 worth of model calls in one night

## Investigation Approach [D05:1]
According to the Runbook: agent latency spike:
1. Confirm the p95 latency rise is real on the dashboard (before stopping at 8-second threshold)
2. Check logs for error patterns like `REG-1009` responses for rate limiting
3. Identify whether the slow service has been ruled out
4. Escalate appropriately if root cause isn't found immediately

The key distinction is that **agent-layer latency usually points to a downstream service issue**, not the agent itself.

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/consoles.md:2" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/consoles.md" title="Consoles and dashboards" section="Consoles and dashboards" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
Instead of trying to represent every piece of data you have, for operational
consoles think of what are the most likely failure modes and how you would use the
consoles to differentiate them. Take advantage of the structure of your
services. For example, if you have a big tree of services in an online-serving
system, latency in some lower service is a typical problem. Rather than showing
every service's information on a single large dashboard, build separate dashboards
for each service that include the latency and errors for each service they talk
to. You can then start at the top and work your way down to the problematic
service.

We have found the following guidelines very effective:
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md:3" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md" title="Alerting" section="Alerting > What to alert on > Online serving systems" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
### Online serving systems

Typically alert on high latency and error rates as high up in the stack as possible.

Only page on latency at one point in a stack. If a lower-level component is
slower than it should be, but the overall user latency is fine, then there is
no need to page.

For error rates, page on user-visible errors. If there are errors further down
the stack that will cause such a failure, there is no need to page on them
separately. However, if some failures are not user-visible, but are otherwise
severe enough to require human involvement (for example, you are losing a lot of
money), add pages to be sent on those.
</source>

<source id="alertmanager/alertmanager.md:2" doc="alertmanager/alertmanager.md" title="Alertmanager" section="Alertmanager > Grouping" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
## Grouping

Grouping categorizes alerts of similar nature into a single notification. This
is especially useful during larger outages when many systems fail at once and
hundreds to thousands of alerts may be firing simultaneously.

content.text:
Based on the company's runbooks and incident reports, here are the most common sources of slowdown during agent latency investigations:

## Primary Causes of Latency

**1. Rate Limiting** [D05:4]
- Agents being rate-limited wait for `Retry-After` headers on every call, which appears as latency in metrics
- This often occurs when another process is sharing the agent's API key

**2. Timeouts Being Treated as Transient Issues** [D09:2]
- A frequent pattern: an external service times out (e.g., payments-gateway checking certificates with auth-service)
- The agent treats timeouts as temporary failures and keeps retrying until it hits its step limit
- Example from INC-2041: An expired intermediate certificate caused payment gateway timeouts, which billing_agent retried continuously

**3. Network Partitions**
- Can occur between services that need to communicate (e.g., alertmanager instances splitting during network partition)
- When services cannot reach databases or each other, requests fail or get stuck waiting

**4. Loop Bugs Without Step Limits** [D13:2]
- Historical example: a loop bug made billing_agent retry failed invoices indefinitely without a cap, exhausting $2,900 worth of model calls in one night

## Investigation Approach [D05:1]
According to the Runbook: agent latency spike:
1. Confirm the p95 latency rise is real on the dashboard (before stopping at 8-second threshold)
2. Check logs for error patterns like `REG-1009` responses for rate limiting
3. Identify whether the slow service has been ruled out
4. Escalate appropriately if root cause isn't found immediately

The key distinction is that **agent-layer latency usually points to a downstream service issue**, not the agent itself.

Look for `REG-1009` responses in the agent's logs. An agent that's being rate-limited waits for `Retry-After` on every call, which looks like latency. If you find them, check whether another process is sharing the agent's key.

</source>

Each agent has a panel with latency, error rate and sessions. The overview dashboard shows every active agent on one screen, sorted by p95. Panels refresh every 30 seconds and lag real time by up to a minute.
</source>

### Online serving systems

Typically alert on high latency and error rates as high up in the stack as possible.

separately. However, if some failures are not user-visible, but are otherwise
severe enough to require human involvement (for example, you are losing a lot of
money), add pages to be sent on those.

content.text:
Based on the company's runbooks and incident reports, here are the most common sources of slowdown during agent latency investigations:

## Primary Causes of Latency

**1. Rate Limiting** [D05:4]
- Agents being rate-limited wait for `Retry-After` headers on every call, which appears as latency in metrics
- This often occurs when another process is sharing the agent's API key

**2. Timeouts Being Treated as Transient Issues** [D09:2]
- A frequent pattern: an external service times out (e.g., payments-gateway checking certificates with auth-service)
- The agent treats timeouts as temporary failures and keeps retrying until it hits its step limit
- Example from INC-2041: An expired intermediate certificate caused payment gateway timeouts, which billing_agent retried continuously

**3. Network Partitions**
- Can occur between services that need to communicate (e.g., alertmanager instances splitting during network partition)
- When services cannot reach databases or each other, requests fail or get stuck waiting

**4. Loop Bugs Without Step Limits** [D13:2]
- Historical example: a loop bug made billing_agent retry failed invoices indefinitely without a cap, exhausting $2,900 worth of model calls in one night

## Investigation Approach [D05:1]
According to the Runbook: agent latency spike:
1. Confirm the p95 latency rise is real on the dashboard (before stopping at 8-second threshold)
2. Check logs for error patterns like `REG-1009` responses for rate limiting
3. Identify whether the slow service has been ruled out
4. Escalate appropriately if root cause isn't found immediately

The key distinction is that **agent-layer latency usually points to a downstream service issue**, not the agent itself.

If you've identified the slow service but don't know who owns it, page the Platform team. Escalation should include the agent name, affected tool, start time, and what you've already ruled out [D05:5].

4. For searches, verify cache health

Based on the registry documentation:

**What a read key can do:**
A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint [D01:1].

**What happens if it tries a write:**
A read key will get error `REG-1004` (FORBIDDEN_FIELD) with an HTTP 403 status code [D02:0]. This error occurs because "The key's scope doesn't allow this change. Writes need a `write` key."

Prometheus integrates with remote storage systems in four ways:

- Prometheus can write samples that it ingests to a remote URL in a Remote Write format.
- Prometheus can receive samples from other clients in a Remote Write format.
- Prometheus can read (back) sample data from a remote URL in a Remote Read format.
- Prometheus can return sample data requested by clients in a Remote Read format.

The remote read and write protocols both use a snappy-compressed protocol buffer encoding over
HTTP. The read protocol is not yet considered as stable API.

The write protocol has a stable specification for 1.0 version
and experimental specification for 2.0 version,
both supported by Prometheus server.
</source>

- Prometheus can write samples that it ingests to a remote URL in a Remote Write format.
- Prometheus can receive samples from other clients in a Remote Write format.
- Prometheus can read (back) sample data from a remote URL in a Remote Read format.
- Prometheus can return sample data requested by clients in a Remote Read format.

The remote read and write protocols both use a snappy-compressed protocol buffer encoding over
HTTP. The read protocol is not yet considered as stable API.

The write protocol has a stable specification for 1.0 version
and experimental specification for 2.0 version,
both supported by Prometheus server.
</source>

<source id="D15:3" doc="D15" title="Wiki: on-call tips" section="Wiki: on-call tips > Paging etiquette" date="2026-09-20" type="wiki">
## Paging etiquette

When you page another team, say what you've already ruled out. "Registry slow, auth-service latency normal, registry-db CPU at 95%" gets a faster answer than "registry slow, please help."
</source>

<source id="D05:5" doc="D05" title="Runbook: agent latency spike" section="Runbook: agent latency spike > Step 5: Escalate" date="2026-07-09" type="official">
## Step 5: Escalate

If you've found the slow service, page its owning team with the agent name, the tool, the start time and what you've ruled out. If you haven't, page Platform. Don't restart the agent to "see if it helps": a restart drops the sessions in progress and hides the evidence.
</source>

<source id="D09:1" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Timeline" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Timeline

- 06:02 — `AgentErrorRateHigh` fired for `billing_agent`. No page: it was outside paging hours.
- 08:00 — The on-call engineer saw the alert and found every failed session stuck on the same payments-gateway call.
- 08:40 — The Payments team found that payments-gateway couldn't open connections to auth-service.
- 08:55 — The Identity team renewed the certificate. `billing_agent` recovered within two minutes.
</source>

<source id="D10:3" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What we changed" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## What we changed

- kb-search's cache settings are now reviewed like code, and a time-to-live above 24 hours needs the Search team's approval.
- Each kb-search result now carries the date the article was last updated, and `research_agent` includes it when it cites a source.
- Reports produced during the affected week were flagged to their readers.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/the_zen.md:15" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/the_zen.md" title="The Zen of Prometheus" section="The Zen of Prometheus > Symptom-based alerts for paging, cause-based for troubleshooting" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
## Symptom-based alerts for paging, cause-based for troubleshooting

Similar to Measure what users care about, alert on what *really* matters. It doesn't matter if your CPU is saturated, as long as your users don't notice. Let your SLOs guide your alerting.

Not every alert needs to page someone. Cause-based alerts shouldn't wake anyone up—they should feed into dashboards or ticket queues to be checked when needed or handled in batches at leisure. Reserve paging for symptom-based alerts that indicate user-facing impact.

For more context My Philosophy on Alerting.
</source>

## Reading one agent

`GET /agents/{agent_id}` returns one agent's full record, or `REG-1005` if no agent has that id.

```json
{
  "agent_id": "research_agent",
  "model": "claude-legacy",
  "tier": "standard",
  "owner": "research-team",
  "status": "active",
  "updated_at": "2026-06-23T09:12:44Z"
}
```

`GET /agents/me` returns the agent that owns the key making the request. It's the quickest way to check that a newly deployed key works and belongs to the agent you expect.
</source>

## Core services

- **registry-api** — the Registry API. Stores every agent's configuration. Owned by the Platform team.
- **registry-db** — the Postgres database behind registry-api, with a hot standby for failover. Owned by the Platform team.
- **auth-service** — validates registry keys and issues the internal certificates services use to talk to each other. Owned by the Identity team.
- **monitoring** — collects latency and error metrics for every agent and raises alerts. Owned by the Observability team.
- **kb-search** — search over the internal knowledge base, with a response cache in front of it. Owned by the Search team.

<source id="D10:1" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What happened" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## What happened

`research_agent` finds its sources through kb-search. On 2026-06-15 a config change set the kb-search cache's time-to-live to 7 days instead of 7 hours. Every search that had been cached returned the version of each article from when it was first cached, so answers drifted further out of date each day.
</source>

<source id="D10:3" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What we changed" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## What we changed

- kb-search's cache settings are now reviewed like code, and a time-to-live above 24 hours needs the Search team's approval.
- Each kb-search result now carries the date the article was last updated, and `research_agent` includes it when it cites a source.
- Reports produced during the affected week were flagged to their readers.
</source>

content.text:
Based on the documentation, if the search service **kb-search** that `research_agent` relies on is slow, you should page the **Search team**.

From the agent platform architecture [D04:1], kb-search is "search over the internal knowledge base, with a response cache in front of it. Owned by the Search team."

The incident INC-2067 [D10:1] confirmed that `research_agent` "finds its sources through kb-search," and when kb-search's cache settings were changed incorrectly, it caused outdated results in research_agent's answers.

Per paging etiquette [D05:5], when you've identified the slow service, page its owning team along with the agent name, the tool, the start time, and what you've ruled out.

If you've found the slow service, page its owning team with the agent name, the tool, the start time and what you've ruled out. If you haven't, page Platform. Don't restart the agent to "see if it helps": a restart drops the sessions in progress and hides the evidence.

## Symptom-based alerts for paging, cause-based for troubleshooting

Similar to Measure what users care about, alert on what *really* matters. It doesn't matter if your CPU is saturated, as long as your users don't notice. Let your SLOs guide your alerting.

Not every alert needs to page someone. Cause-based alerts shouldn't wake anyone up—they should feed into dashboards or ticket queues to be checked when needed or handled in batches at leisure. Reserve paging for symptom-based alerts that indicate user-facing impact.

For more context My Philosophy on Alerting.
</source>

<source id="D01:3" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Reading one agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Reading one agent

`GET /agents/{agent_id}` returns one agent's full record, or `REG-1005` if no agent has that id.

```json
{
  "agent_id": "research_agent",
  "model": "claude-legacy",
  "tier": "standard",
  "owner": "research-team",
  "status": "active",
  "updated_at": "2026-06-23T09:12:44Z"
}
```

`GET /agents/me` returns the agent that owns the key making the request. It's the quickest way to check that a newly deployed key works and belongs to the agent you expect.
</source>

## Who to contact

Page the owning team through the on-call rota: Platform for registry-api and registry-db, Identity for auth-service, Observability for monitoring, and Search for kb-search.
</source>

<source id="D04:1" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > Core services" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## Core services

- **registry-api** — the Registry API. Stores every agent's configuration. Owned by the Platform team.
- **registry-db** — the Postgres database behind registry-api, with a hot standby for failover. Owned by the Platform team.
- **auth-service** — validates registry keys and issues the internal certificates services use to talk to each other. Owned by the Identity team.
- **monitoring** — collects latency and error metrics for every agent and raises alerts. Owned by the Observability team.
- **kb-search** — search over the internal knowledge base, with a response cache in front of it. Owned by the Search team.
</source>

<source id="D05:3" doc="D05" title="Runbook: agent latency spike" section="Runbook: agent latency spike > Step 3: Check the cache hit rate" date="2026-07-09" type="official">
## Step 3: Check the cache hit rate

If the slow tool is a search, check the cache hit rate on its panel. Below 40% usually means the cache was flushed or restarted, and it refills on its own within about 10 minutes. Wait that long before escalating. If the hit rate stays low after 10 minutes, the cache itself may be misconfigured.
</source>

## What happened

`research_agent` finds its sources through kb-search. On 2026-06-15 a config change set the kb-search cache's time-to-live to 7 days instead of 7 hours. Every search that had been cached returned the version of each article from when it was first cached, so answers drifted further out of date each day.
</source>

<source id="D10:3" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What we changed" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## What we changed

- kb-search's cache settings are now reviewed like code, and a time-to-live above 24 hours needs the Search team's approval.
- Each kb-search result now carries the date the article was last updated, and `research_agent` includes it when it cites a source.
- Reports produced during the affected week were flagged to their readers.
</source>

<source id="D04:3" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > The agents that use them" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## The agents that use them

`support_agent` answers customer questions. It looks up agent and account configuration through registry-api and searches help articles through kb-search. `triage_agent` reads incoming tickets and hands the ones it can't close to `support_agent`.
</source>

<source id="D04:2" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > How requests flow" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## How requests flow

When a request reaches registry-api, it first asks auth-service to validate the `X-Registry-Key` header, then reads or writes registry-db. If auth-service is slow, every registry request is slow; if registry-db is unavailable, registry-api can't answer at all.

Monitoring gets its list of agents from registry-api every 30 seconds, then collects metrics from each agent on the list.
</source>

<source id="D07:1" doc="D07" title="Runbook: migrating agents off claude-legacy" section="Runbook: migrating agents off claude-legacy > Which agents are affected" date="2026-07-02" type="official">

| `research_agent` | research-team | `claude-sonnet` |
| `notes_agent` | support-team | `claude-haiku` |

Owners can check any agent with `GET /agents/{agent_id}` and look at its `model` field.

<source id="D11:2" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What made it worse" date="2026-08-29" type="official">

## Packaging and dependencies

Ideally, a client library can be included in any application to add some
instrumentation without breaking the application.

Accordingly, caution is advised when adding dependencies to the client library.
For example, if you add a library that uses a Prometheus client that requires
version x.y of a library but the application uses x.z elsewhere, will that have
an adverse impact on the application?

It is suggested that where this may arise, that the core instrumentation is
separated from the bridges/exposition of metrics in a given format. For

## Packaging and dependencies

Ideally, a client library can be included in any application to add some
instrumentation without breaking the application.

Accordingly, caution is advised when adding dependencies to the client library.
For example, if you add a library that uses a Prometheus client that requires
version x.y of a library but the application uses x.z elsewhere, will that have
an adverse impact on the application?

It is suggested that where this may arise, that the core instrumentation is
separated from the bridges/exposition of metrics in a given format. For
example, the Java simpleclient `simpleclient` module has no dependencies, and
the `simpleclient_servlet` has the HTTP bits.
</source>

## What made it worse

## What we changed

- An alert now fires when the standby falls more than 60 seconds behind.

- 14:52 — The standby finished catching up and registry-api recovered. The queued tickets were handed over by 15:05.

<source id="D01:7" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Tiers and models" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Tiers and models

Every agent has a tier, and each tier allows a fixed set of models:

| Tier | Allowed models |
|---|---|
| `standard` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet` |
| `priority` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet`, `claude-opus` |

Moving an agent to `claude-opus` therefore means moving it to the `priority` tier first, which needs approval from its owner's budget holder. `claude-legacy` is deprecated and can't be assigned to any agent; existing agents on it keep working until 2026-10-31.
</source>

<source id="D14:1" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > Can my agent use the biggest model?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">
## Can my agent use the biggest model?

Only on the priority tier. Standard-tier agents can use the smaller and mid-sized models. Moving to priority needs a sign-off from whoever holds your team's budget, and after that you can change the model.
</source>

<source id="D07:2" doc="D07" title="Runbook: migrating agents off claude-legacy" section="Runbook: migrating agents off claude-legacy > Step 1: Check the target is allowed" date="2026-07-02" type="official">
## Step 1: Check the target is allowed

Both target models are allowed on the `standard` tier, so neither agent needs a tier change. If you'd rather move to `claude-opus`, the agent must move to the `priority` tier first, or the change fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D03:3" doc="D03" title="Registry changelog" section="Registry changelog > v2.3 — 2026-03-10" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## v2.3 — 2026-03-10

- Added the `tier` field to every agent. Existing agents were set to `standard`.
- Each tier now has an allowlist of models. Assigning a model outside it returns `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D01:4" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Creating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Creating an agent

`POST /agents` creates an agent. It needs a `write` key. The body must include `agent_id`, `model`, `tier` and `owner`; `status` defaults to `active`.

```json
{"agent_id": "triage_agent", "model": "claude-haiku", "tier": "standard", "owner": "support-team"}
```

Agent ids must be unique: reusing one returns `REG-1006`. The model must be allowed on the agent's tier (see "Tiers and models"), or the request fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

Currently, metrics created by the official Prometheus client_golang
library accept UTF-8 names by

boolean is now deprecated and should always be set to UTF8Validation. Legacy

## Configuring Name Validation during Scraping

By default, Prometheus 3.0 accepts all UTF-8 strings as valid metric and label
names. It is possible to override this behavior for scraped targets and reject
names that do not conform to the legacy character set.

This option can be set in the Prometheus YAML file on a global basis:

```yaml
global:
  metric_name_validation_scheme: legacy
```

or on a per-scrape config basis:

```yaml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: prometheus
    metric_name_validation_scheme: legacy
```
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/migration.md:15" doc="prometheus-server/migration.md" title="Prometheus 3.0 migration guide" section="Prometheus 3.0 migration guide > Miscellaneous > UTF-8 names" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
### UTF-8 names

Prometheus v3 supports UTF-8 in metric and label names. This means metric and
label names can change after upgrading according to what is exposed by
endpoints. Furthermore, metric and label names that would have previously been
flagged as invalid no longer will be.

Users wishing to preserve the original validation behavior can update their
Prometheus yaml configuration to specify the legacy validation scheme:

```
global:
  metric_name_validation_scheme: legacy
```

Or on a per-scrape basis:

```
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: job1
    metric_name_validation_scheme: utf8
  - job_name: job2
    metric_name_validation_scheme: legacy
```
</source>

## Configuring Name Validation during Scraping

By default, Prometheus 3.0 accepts all UTF-8 strings as valid metric and label
names. It is possible to override this behavior for scraped targets and reject
names that do not conform to the legacy character set.

This option can be set in the Prometheus YAML file on a global basis:

```yaml
global:
  metric_name_validation_scheme: legacy
```

or on a per-scrape config basis:

```yaml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: prometheus
    metric_name_validation_scheme: legacy
```

Prometheus v3 supports UTF-8 in metric and label names. This means metric and
label names can change after upgrading according to what is exposed by

global:

This should return a number of different time series (along with the latest value
recorded for each), each with the metric name

labels designate different latency percentiles and target group intervals.

query:

prometheus_target_interval_length_seconds{quantile="0.99"}

To count the number of returned time series, you could write:

count(prometheus_target_interval_length_seconds)

For more about the expression language, see the

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/histograms.md:46" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/histograms.md" title="Histograms and summaries" section="Histograms and summaries > Quantiles > Errors of quantile estimation" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
### Errors of quantile estimation

Next step in our thought experiment: A change in backend routing
adds a fixed amount of 100ms to all request durations. Now the request
duration has its sharp spike at 320ms.

The relevant bucket of the native histogram ranges from 297ms to 324ms (again
just stating numbers here without telling you how they are calculated), with
the interpolated estimation for the 95th percentile being 323ms. That's an
almost perfect guess.

The classic histogram, however, will see almost all observations in the bucket
from 300ms to 450ms. The 95th percentile is estimated to be 443ms, far away
from the correct value close to 320ms. While you are only a tiny bit outside of
your SLO, the estimated 95th quantile looks much worse.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/histograms.md:32" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/histograms.md" title="Histograms and summaries" section="Histograms and summaries > Quantiles" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
## Quantiles

You can use both summaries and histograms to calculate so-called φ-quantiles,
where 0 ≤ φ ≤ 1. The φ-quantile is the observation value that ranks at number
φ*N among the N observations. Examples for φ-quantiles: The 0.5-quantile is
known as the median. The 0.95-quantile is also called the 95th percentile.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/histograms.md:45" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/histograms.md" title="Histograms and summaries" section="Histograms and summaries > Quantiles > Errors of quantile estimation" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
### Errors of quantile estimation

Now let's apply the same to the classic histogram configured as described
above. All observations, and therefore also the 95th percentile, will fall into
the bucket labeled `{le="0.3"}`, i.e. the bucket from 200ms to 300ms. The
interpolation would estimate 295ms in this case, with the guarantee that the
true value is between 200ms and 300ms. Not only is the error margin much
larger, also the estimated value of 295ms is much farther away from the true
value of 220ms than in case of the native histogram, where the estimation was
228ms. Given that the SLO is at 300ms for the 95th percentile, the classic
histogram gives you the impression that you are very close to breaching it, but
in reality you are still doing quite well.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/histograms.md:49" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/histograms.md" title="Histograms and summaries" section="Histograms and summaries > Quantiles > Errors of quantile estimation" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
### Errors of quantile estimation

Let us now modify the experiment once more. In the new setup, the distributions
of request durations has a spike at 150ms, but it is not quite as sharp as
before and only comprises 90% of the observations. 10% of the observations are
evenly spread out in a long tail between 150ms and 450ms. With that
distribution, the 95th percentile happens to be exactly at our SLO of 300ms.
With the classic histogram, the calculated value would be accurate in this
(contrived) case, as the value of the 95th percentile happens to coincide with
one of the configured bucket boundaries. Even slightly different values would
still be accurate as the even distribution within the relevant buckets is
exactly what the interpolation algorithm for classic histograms assumes.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/histograms.md:50" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/histograms.md" title="Histograms and summaries" section="Histograms and summaries > Quantiles > Errors of quantile estimation" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
### Errors of quantile estimation

The error of the quantile reported by a summary gets more interesting here. In
the case of the Go instrumentation library, the error of the quantile in a
summary is configured in the dimension of φ. In our case we might have
configured 0.95±0.01, i.e. the calculated value will be between the 94th and
96th percentile. The 94th quantile with the distribution described above is
270ms, the 96th quantile is 330ms. The calculated value of the 95th percentile
reported by the summary can be anywhere in the interval between 270ms and
330ms, which unfortunately is all the difference between clearly within the SLO
vs. clearly outside the SLO.
</source>

The available documentation describes kb-search as "search over the internal knowledge base, with a response cache in front of it" [D04:1], owned by the Search team. However, no explicit latency SLA or target (such as p95 latency in milliseconds or seconds) is documented for this service.

There is a general p95 latency target mentioned elsewhere - the `AgentLatencyHigh` alert fires when an agent's p95 response time stays above 8 seconds for 10 minutes [D05:0] - but this applies to agents using the platform, not to kb-search infrastructure itself.

If you need the specific latency target for kb-search, this information would likely be maintained by the Observability team (who collects metrics for all services) or the Search team (the owners of kb-search). You may want to consult their runbooks or directly ask them via the on-call rota.

## What happened

<source id="D04:1" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > Core services" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## Core services

- **registry-api** — the Registry API. Stores every agent's configuration. Owned by the Platform team.
- **registry-db** — the Postgres database behind registry-api, with a hot standby for failover. Owned by the Platform team.
- **auth-service** — validates registry keys and issues the internal certificates services use to talk to each other. Owned by the Identity team.
- **monitoring** — collects latency and error metrics for every agent and raises alerts. Owned by the Observability team.
- **kb-search** — search over the internal knowledge base, with a response cache in front of it. Owned by the Search team.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/getting_started.md:7" doc="prometheus-server/getting_started.md" title="Getting started" section="Getting started > Using the expression browser" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
## Using the expression browser

This should return a number of different time series (along with the latest value
recorded for each), each with the metric name
`prometheus_target_interval_length_seconds`, but with different labels. These
labels designate different latency percentiles and target group intervals.

If we are interested only in 99th percentile latencies, we could use this
query:

```
prometheus_target_interval_length_seconds{quantile="0.99"}
```

To count the number of returned time series, you could write:

```
count(prometheus_target_interval_length_seconds)
```

For more about the expression language, see the
expression language documentation.
</source>

<source id="D05:1" doc="D05" title="Runbook: agent latency spike" section="Runbook: agent latency spike > Step 1: Confirm it on the dashboard" date="2026-07-09" type="official">
## Step 1: Confirm it on the dashboard

Open the agent's latency panel and check that the rise is real and still happening. A single slow session can trip a short-lived spike that recovers before you get there. If p95 is back under 8 seconds, note it in the alert thread and stop.
</source>

<source id="D08:3" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > Dashboards" date="2026-03-02" type="official">
## Dashboards

Each agent has a panel with latency, error rate and sessions. The overview dashboard shows every active agent on one screen, sorted by p95. Panels refresh every 30 seconds and lag real time by up to a minute.
</source>

<source id="D05:0" doc="D05" title="Runbook: agent latency spike" section="Runbook: agent latency spike > When to use this runbook" date="2026-07-09" type="official">
## When to use this runbook

Use it when the `AgentLatencyHigh` alert fires for an agent, or when users report that an agent is taking much longer than usual to answer. The alert fires when an agent's p95 response time stays above 8 seconds for 10 minutes.
</source>
